comparator.name: Oudheidwetenschappen
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from VU Amsterdam's (and UvA's, as joint ACASA partner) current official sources for the Fall-2026 cohort: the Oudheidwetenschappen programme content page, the programme's toekomst/career page, and the Bachelor's programme Ancient Studies 2026-2027 Teaching and Examination Regulations (OER/TER), the formally adopted joint VU/UvA regulation governing both the Dutch-taught 'Oudheidwetenschappen' track and the English-taught 'Ancient Studies' track of the same ACASA programme (Article 7.1: RIO number RIO56704 for both VU and UvA). Article 10.4 confirms the language of instruction and examination for the Oudheidwetenschappen track is Dutch, matching the registry's normalized languages_json (['NLD']); this reconstruction therefore follows the Dutch-taught track. Article 10.2 confirms the programme offers five specialisations under the Oudheidwetenschappen track: Oude Geschiedenis (Ancient History), Oude Nabije Oosten (Ancient Near Eastern Studies), Archeologie (Archaeology), Grieks and Latijn. Article 11.1 requires every student to complete exactly one 30-EC compulsory specialisation (post-propaedeutic phase: 78 EC disciplinary/interdisciplinary courses + at least 30 EC elective components + a 12-EC thesis); no specialisation is formally designated as the generic or default track. Because the normalized target does not itself name a specific specialisation and no specialisation is formally more general than the others (each is an equally-weighted 30-EC compulsory choice under Article 11.6), the least-specialised-pair test under the route-selection rule was applied: Ancient History and Archaeology are the two broadest of the five specialisations in subject-matter terms, since both range across periods, regions and forms of evidence rather than being anchored to acquisition of a single ancient language (unlike Ancient Near Eastern Studies, Grieks and Latijn, each of which presupposes a dedicated language-acquisition sequence under Articles 11.4 and 11.6). Between Ancient History and Archaeology, Article 10.2 itself lists the five specialisations in a fixed order -- Oude Geschiedenis, Oude Nabije Oosten, Archeologie, Grieks, Latijn -- placing Oude Geschiedenis before Archeologie; this order was used as the neutral tie-break, and Oude Geschiedenis (Ancient History) was therefore selected as the reconstructed specialisation. This selection was fixed before any UCR course was considered and does not depend on UCR fit. Article 2.2.1 and Article 11.1 establish the frame programme: a 60-EC propaedeutic year (Article 11.3: 48 EC of eight compulsory 6-EC units of education, plus Article 11.4: 12 EC from two 6-EC 'exploratory units of education (electives)... to orientate on the specialisation', chosen here as Seminar Ancient History and Classical Mythology, both drawn from the official orientation-elective list for Oudheidwetenschappen-track students and consistent with the selected Ancient History specialisation and the programme content page's own evidence for classical mythology as first-year content); and 120 post-propaedeutic EC (Article 2.2.1.b) comprising 78 EC of disciplinary/interdisciplinary courses (Article 11.5's eight 6-EC common post-propaedeutic units, totalling 48 EC, plus Article 11.6's five 6-EC Oude Geschiedenis specialisation units, totalling 30 EC), at least 30 EC of genuinely open elective/minor space (Article 12.1, preserved here as open space rather than instantiated with invented content, consistent with its explicitly open, multi-option design: a minor, an individual choice of units of education, study abroad, or an internship), and a 12-EC Bachelorscriptie Oudheidwetenschappen (Article 11.5; Article 9.1's interim-examination sequencing rule permits the thesis only once all first- and second-year units are completed). Article 11.5's post-propaedeutic common unit 'Receptie en Creatief Schrijven / Classical Reception and Creative Writing' is track-specific; the Dutch-taught 'Receptie en Creatief Schrijven' (L_AABAXGO201) is used here consistent with the selected Dutch-taught track. No OER article or further official source needed to be consulted beyond the programme content page, the OER/TER and the career page: together they establish a complete, internally consistent, entirely accounted-for 180-EC pathway with explicit EC weights and compulsory/elective status for every component, and an explicit, UCR-independent route-selection judgment fixed before any UCR course was considered.

routeSelection.basis: OER Article 10.2 lists five specialisations under the Oudheidwetenschappen track (Oude Geschiedenis, Oude Nabije Oosten, Archeologie, Grieks, Latijn) and Article 11.1 requires exactly one 30-EC compulsory specialisation; none is formally the generic/default option. Ancient History and Archaeology are the least specialised of the five (neither presupposes acquisition of a specific ancient language, unlike Ancient Near Eastern Studies, Grieks and Latijn), so under the route-selection rule's least-specialised-general step they were treated as the two candidates remaining. Article 10.2's own listed order then places Oude Geschiedenis before Archeologie, and this official curriculum order was used as the neutral tie-break between them per the route-selection rule's final step. The selection was fixed before any UCR course was considered and does not depend on UCR fit.

Working with both material (archaeological) and textual (literary, documentary) evidence of antiquity
Ancient history: political systems, empires, multicultural societies and international relations in antiquity, as the specific Oude Geschiedenis specialisation reconstructed for this target
Using antiquity to understand and illuminate present-day society, politics and culture
Identity, migration and cultural contact across history, including contact between the Near East and the Greco-Roman/Western world
The classical canon, heritage and how cultures select, remember and reuse antiquity, including the afterlife and reception of classical cultures
Classical mythology as substantive interdisciplinary first-year content
Ancient philosophy as part of the interdisciplinary first-year foundation, and the classical roots of Western philosophical and political thought
Creative and literary reception of ancient texts and narratives
Historical and source-critical research methods integrated throughout the curriculum
Academic writing, oral presentation and argumentation skills integrated throughout the curriculum

questions: What can the epics of Gilgamesh, Homer and Virgil tell us about how ancient societies told their own origin stories?

How does Herodotus' account of antiquity compare with the mythic tradition of the Trojan War?

selection.assessment: The closest match directly owns ten generator-eligible rows: the defining Mediterranean/Near-Eastern cultural field and its five-discipline interdisciplinary combination of archaeology, literature, philosophy, history and mythology (5032, 5036); using antiquity to understand present-day society (5033); identity and migration across history and cultural contact between East and West (5034, 5035); working with material and textual evidence (5037); ancient history itself as the selected specialisation, together with its own political-systems/international-relations and multicultural-societies content (5039, 5043, 5044); and the afterlife/reception of classical cultures (5055). The remaining six generator-eligible rows describe VU's other four specialisations and were independently assessed as three candidate directions. Archaeology (5038, supported by 5045 and 5051, itself an archaeology-adjacent curricular-topic row on burial practices) is a genuine, formally distinct 30-EC specialisation, but UCR's entire archaeology/heritage-adjacent catalogue -- Introduction to World Archaeology, Greek Archaeology, Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Heritage & Ancient Democracy and Writing Art's Histories -- is already fully used by the closest match to reconstruct the programme's shared interdisciplinary core, because these are the only heritage/archaeology-adjacent courses UCR's actual catalogue contains. A second alternative built around Archaeology as its own organising direction would therefore either reuse the closest match's own heritage courses (there is no separate archaeological-method or fieldwork course to substitute), falling well short of the required 30-EC/4-course floor once the closest match's necessarily-overlapping Literature, History and Philosophy courses are also considered, or import courses from outside the evidenced field merely to force numerical distinctness. Latin and Greek (5040, 5041, clustered because both describe the same substantive gap -- UCR teaches no ancient language -- and the same closest-available UCR response) are dedicated language-and-literature specialisations; the only available UCR response, engaging classical literature, myth and rhetoric in translation, is precisely the Literature and Rhetoric/Communication cluster (nine of the closest match's own 24 courses) that the closest match already uses in full. Akkadian and Ancient Near Eastern Studies (5042) fares worse still: UCR's catalogue contains no course addressing cuneiform writing, the Akkadian language or Mesopotamian civilisation specifically; the only tangentially relevant content (Introduction to World Archaeology's brief treatment of early Near Eastern sites) is already fully consumed by the closest match and does not constitute a defensible specialist offering in its own right. Because each candidate's own evidence is already substantively covered by the closest match's exhausted use of UCR's small relevant catalogue, and no genuinely different 24-course curriculum follows from any of them given UCR's actual course offerings, all three are rejected -- Archaeology and Latin/Greek as not-substantively-distinct, Akkadian/Ancient Near Eastern Studies as insufficient-evidence -- rather than manufactured through arbitrary course substitution, and production stops at one included alternative.

alternatives.label: The Ancient World: Heritage, Literature & History
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is built from UCR's full available heritage/archaeology/art-history cluster (6 of 24 courses: Introduction to World Archaeology, Greek Archaeology, Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Heritage & Ancient Democracy and Writing Art's Histories), its literature and rhetoric/communication courses considered together (9 of 24: five Literature courses covering ancient epic, myth and reception, and four Rhetoric/Communication courses explicitly rooted in the classical rhetorical tradition), its history courses (3 of 24, covering empires, ancient/pre-modern warfare and historical research method), and a smaller philosophy, political-philosophy and research-methods complement (5 of 24), plus Personal & Professional Development. The label names Heritage first because archaeology, art history and heritage/canon-formation form UCR's single largest disciplinary cluster in the completed programme and the strongest available substitute for the Archaeology-specialisation content this Ancient-History-route reconstruction does not itself reproduce; Literature second because UCR's literature and rhetoric courses, considered together, are the numerically largest combined strand and the closest available substitute for VU's Latin/Greek literary specialisations, which UCR cannot reproduce in the original languages; and History third for the Oude Geschiedenis specialisation content -- empires, ancient warfare, political thought and historical method -- that most directly reconstructs VU's own selected route. It does not claim dedicated instruction in Latin, Greek, Akkadian or any other ancient language, a formal Archaeology-specialisation fieldwork component, or a religion-in-antiquity course, none of which the completed 24-course curriculum contains.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to VU/UvA's Oudheidwetenschappen bachelor under its Oude Geschiedenis (Ancient History) specialisation (OER Articles 10.2, 11.1, 11.6). It reproduces as far as UCR's actual catalogue allows the programme's interdisciplinary first-year foundation across archaeology/material culture, literature and mythology, philosophy and cultural history (the programme's own explicit five-field combination of art, literature, philosophy, history and mythology), the working-with-material-and-textual-evidence method that recurs throughout the curriculum, and the Ancient History specialisation's own content -- ancient political systems, empires, multicultural societies and international relations. Because UCR offers no course in any ancient language (Latin, Greek or Akkadian), no dedicated archaeological-fieldwork course and no religion-in-antiquity course, the concept substitutes UCR's own literature, rhetoric/communication and heritage/art-history clusters for VU's Latin/Greek literary specialisations and dedicated Archaeology-specialisation fieldwork, and its philosophy and political-philosophy courses for the interdisciplinary philosophy-of-the-humanities component, preserving honest gaps rather than compensating with weakly related material.
progression: No UCR course in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite (the enriched database records preq1: NONE for all 24 selected courses), so no formal-prerequisite ordering constraint applies. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 1, within Year 1. Level-1 gateway and introductory courses are concentrated in semesters 1-3 (Personal & Professional Development, Introduction to Literary Studies, Introduction to Western Philosophy, The Art of Rhetorical Communication in semester 1; Introduction to World Archaeology and Great Literary Works in semester 2; Introduction to Political Philosophy and Human Rights: Law & Philosophy in semester 3), while level-3 advanced work is concentrated in semesters 5-6 (Modern Art & Modern Museums, Heritage & Ancient Democracy, Film & Text and Persuasive Communication in semester 5; History Research Seminar, Rhetoric in Action, Perspectives on Literary Meaning and Writing Art's Histories in semester 6), so that foundational humanities training precedes advanced work. Where an advisory continuation exists in the course evidence -- Persuasive Communication explicitly builds on 'existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory' -- The Art of Rhetorical Communication is scheduled in semester 1, well before Persuasive Communication in semester 5. Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.

blocks: Interdisciplinary orientation, material culture, philosophy & research skills

Both address ancient material culture and objects: Objects in Context is VU's interdisciplinary introduction to the ancient world through its objects; Introduction to World Archaeology examines how making and using objects defined human existence and societies from earliest beginnings to the end of antiquity.

Both provide a broad chronological/cultural overview of the ancient Near East and Greek world through their literary and cultural monuments: Cultural History of the Ancient World 1 is VU's own broad survey; Great Literary Works opens with the epic of Gilgamesh and surveys the ancient literary canon.

Both address the Hellenistic, Italian and Roman world through the lens of conflict and power: Cultural History of the Ancient World 2 surveys this broad cultural-historical territory; Western Way of War gives a chronological account of warfare in the Western world from antiquity, when this territory was contested and shaped by war.

Both are the introductory philosophy course covering the ancient philosophical tradition: Ancient Philosophy is VU's own dedicated first-year unit; Introduction to Western Philosophy introduces central philosophical themes over 2,500 years, beginning with antiquity.

Both train the critical use of primary evidence: Historical Sources is VU's practical exercise in working with primary source material; History Research Seminar guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, including engaging critically with sources and archival research.

Seminar Ancient History is an orientation elective specifically introducing historical inquiry into antiquity, chosen to orientate toward the selected Ancient History specialisation. UCR's own history-research-methods course, History Research Seminar, is already aligned to the comparator's Historical Sources component above and cannot be matched twice, so no further counterpart is claimed.
Heritage, canon formation & the reception of antiquity

Both concern how the heritage and canon of antiquity has been constructed and interpreted over time: The Classical Canon 1 introduces the heritage of antiquity; Writing Art's Histories traces the history of art history as a discipline and how scholars have interpreted and canonised art since the sixteenth century.

Both concern cultural contact and exchange across the Mediterranean and between East and West: Cultural Contact: East and West is VU's own dedicated first-year unit; Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean examines the artistic connections linking Italy to the wider Mediterranean, including the Islamic eastern Mediterranean.

Both concern the afterlife and adaptation of source texts across media and periods: Classics Beyond Antiquity studies how ancient culture has been received in later periods; Film & Text studies the adaptation, intertextuality and reception of literary texts in film.

Both are dedicated courses in classical and world mythology: Classical Mythology is VU's own orientation elective; World Myth & Literature investigates ancient literary myths, including Greek myths, alongside other mythic traditions.

Both concern how societies select and present cultural heritage: The Classical Canon 2 examines the sociology of cultural selection; Modern Art & Modern Museums examines how museums and exhibitions curate, select and present art and heritage.

Both concern how texts are received and reinterpreted through different critical lenses: Receptie en Creatief Schrijven (Classical Reception and Creative Writing) studies the creative reception of ancient texts; Perspectives on Literary Meaning examines how humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic perspectives affect the reading and interpretation of texts.

Lieux de mémoire is a dedicated course on how antiquity is remembered in places. UCR's heritage/reception-adjacent courses are already matched above and cannot be matched twice; UCR offers no course specifically on sites of memory, so no further counterpart is claimed.
Ancient history, political thought & the Ancient Near East

Both examine the rise and fall of ancient empires: The Decline and Fall of Rome is VU's compulsory Ancient History specialisation unit on Rome; History of Empires examines the rise, fall and contested nature of empires through major historical examples.

Both examine ancient and classical political thought: Politics and International Relations in Antiquity is VU's compulsory Ancient History specialisation unit; Introduction to Political Philosophy examines the views of influential Western thinkers, including classical political philosophers, on society and political authority.

Both critically examine ancient political institutions and their modern reception: Past and Present: Critical Approaches to Antiquity and Archaeological Heritage is VU's dedicated critical-approaches unit; Heritage & Ancient Democracy returns to the roots of ancient Greek democracy and its modern heritage reception.

History and Culture of the Ancient Near East is a compulsory Ancient History specialisation unit on Near Eastern civilisation specifically. UCR's Introduction to World Archaeology touches the early Near East only briefly and is already matched to Objects in Context above; UCR offers no dedicated Ancient Near Eastern history course, so no further counterpart is claimed.

Cultural Contact: Mediterranean Connections is a further post-propaedeutic unit on Mediterranean cultural exchange. UCR's Mediterranean-contact course, Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean, is already matched to Cultural Contact: East and West above and cannot be matched twice, so no further counterpart is claimed.

In search of the Masses of Antiquity is a compulsory Ancient History specialisation unit on the social history of ordinary people in antiquity. UCR offers no course specifically on the social history of the ancient masses, so no counterpart is claimed.

World Heritage and Conflict is a compulsory Ancient History specialisation unit. UCR's heritage-and-conflict-adjacent courses are already matched above and cannot be matched twice, so no further counterpart is claimed.
Philosophy of the humanities & religion in antiquity

Both are the programme's second philosophy-oriented unit, extending beyond introductory ancient philosophy: Philosophy of the Humanities (ACASA) is VU's interdisciplinary philosophy-of-science unit; Ethics explores theories of moral reasoning, including virtue ethics rooted in ancient philosophical traditions.
Religion in Antiquity is a dedicated course on ancient religion and cult. UCR offers no religion course of any kind, so no counterpart is claimed.
ACASA Excursion is a practical fieldwork/excursion component. UCR offers no equivalent fieldwork or excursion unit for this concept, so no counterpart is claimed.

The 30-EC year-3 vrije keuzeruimte (a programmed minor, an individual choice of units of education, study abroad, or an internship) is genuine open profiling space with no fixed content specified by VU/UvA. It is preserved as open space and not matched to any UCR course.

Bachelorscriptie Oudheidwetenschappen is the 12-EC independent interdisciplinary bachelor thesis (OER Article 9.1 requires all first- and second-year units to be completed before enrolment). No scheduled UCR course is a thesis; UCR's standardised Optional independent research element is shown in this row instead, consistent with researchComponentId.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial interdisciplinary study of the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world through archaeology/heritage, literature and mythology, philosophy and history. The Oudheidwetenschappen bachelor additionally includes specialist work in Latin, Greek and Akkadian language and literature (dedicated language-acquisition sequences), religion in antiquity, and Ancient-History-specialisation fieldwork/excursion and Ancient-Near-East components. UCR students can instead combine UCR's heritage/archaeology, literature, rhetoric, history and philosophy courses, but UCR offers no course in any ancient language, no religion-in-antiquity course, and no archaeological fieldwork or excursion component, so those specialist components are not offered at UCR at any level of depth.
